buildSteps.title: Choose a chip that can be documented
buildSteps.detail: Everything depends on picking a processor whose datasheet and registers can be published without a non-disclosure agreement, and whose support can be merged into the mainline Linux kernel. Most mobile chips fail this test, so the choice is narrow.

buildSteps.title: Design the mainboard
buildSteps.detail: Engineers draw the schematic and lay out the printed circuit board with free design tools, putting the cellular modem on a socketed module so a single component can be replaced or upgraded later.

buildSteps.title: Publish the design
buildSteps.detail: Schematic, board files, bill of materials and mechanical drawings are released under an open licence before manufacturing, so others can inspect, correct and re-spin them.

buildSteps.title: Bring up prototypes
buildSteps.detail: A handful of boards are assembled by a quick-turn service; developers then write or fix drivers for the display, touch, modem and power management until the device boots and runs a standard kernel.

buildSteps.title: Design the case and tooling
buildSteps.detail: The case is 3D-printed through several iterations, then a steel mould is cut for injection moulding, or the design is kept small enough for machining and 3D printing by users.

buildSteps.title: Certify the device
buildSteps.detail: The finished design must pass radio-emissions, electrical-safety and cellular-network approval — an expensive step that must be budgeted before any production run.

buildSteps.title: Run a small production batch
buildSteps.detail: A contract manufacturer populates and tests the boards, the units are assembled with battery and screen, and each one is flashed and functionally tested before shipping.

buildSteps.title: Maintain and supply spares
buildSteps.detail: The hard part after launch: keep kernel support current, sell screens, batteries and boards individually for years, and hand the design to a community that can keep producing it.

prerequisites.why: without register-level documentation, no one outside the chip vendor can write or maintain a driver.

prerequisites.tech: Mainline kernel support for mobile chips
prerequisites.why: several phone chips now boot a stock kernel, but camera, modem and power management often lag for years.
baseband firmware remains proprietary, so even a fully open phone relies on a closed black box.
contract manufacturers can build a few thousand boards cheaply, which is what makes niche devices possible at all.
projects such as Phosh and Plasma Mobile provide usable shells, but app polish and battery life still trail mainstream phones.

pathway.milestone: niche open handhelds like the PinePhone and Librem 5 ship in thousands, running community distributions such as postmarketOS
pathway.unlocks: proof that a repairable, openly documented pocket computer can be bought and used daily, with real compromises.

pathway.milestone: better-documented SoCs and faster mainline bring-up
pathway.unlocks: porting a new device drops from years to months, letting more small makers enter the market.

pathway.milestone: modular designs with a published parts list and guaranteed spares
pathway.unlocks: a device that can be upgraded and repaired for a decade instead of replaced every three years.

pathway.milestone: repairability rules and interoperable modules spread to mainstream handsets
pathway.unlocks: open-hardware practice moves from hobby scale into ordinary consumer devices.
